newsitem.title: ITALY: Hard-left urges Italian govt to fight reform vote.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left urges Italian govt to fight reform vote.

text.p: Italy's hard-left Communist Refoundation party called on the government on Thursday to fight a recommendation that the country should adopt a presidential-style electoral system.
Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in parliament, hinted at trouble unless the ruling centre-left coalition worked together to sink the idea.

The recommendation has come from a 70-member parliamentary commission which was set up earlier this year to map out desperately-needed constitutional reform in a bid to halt the revolving-door governments which have plagued Italy since World War Two.
In a key vote in the commission on Wednesday, centre-right opposition parties succeeded in getting backing for the direct election of a president, who will govern alongside a parliamentary premier.
Centre-left parties wanted to reinforce the powers of the prime minister and leave the president with a largely symbolic role, as is currently the case.
"We will fight this battle to the end," warned Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti.
Italy's constitution was worked out some 50 years ago after the fall of fascism and was designed to prevent one person from taking too much power.
However the electoral law has helped create a fragmented, weak political landscape, with modern Italian governments lasting on average only 11 months.

The latest drive to reform the constitution is the third attempt of its kind in 15 years and the proposals that emerge from the cross-party commission will be debated by the full parliament and eventually put to a national referendum.

Centre-left parties looked poised to get their own project approved by the commission, but the vote went against them at the last moment when the separatist Northern League party joined centre-right ranks.
League leader Umberto Bossi said afterwards his party did not want to see a semi-presidential system introduced, but instead wanted to cause the government discomfort.
Many newspaper commentators called the vote a farce and said there were no guarantees that semi-presidentialism would give Italy the kind of political stability it needed.

Under the plan, a president would be directly elected by the people and given a five-year mandate, but could be voted out of office at any time by parliament, so long as there was a two-thirds majority in favour.

The president would be given the power to appoint the prime minister and also have the power to dissolve parliament, but only one or two years after general elections. The prime minister would set the day-to-day political agenda.

Amendments to the proposals will be discussed by the commission over the next month, with Refoundation vowing to change the nature of the package. The recommendations will then be passed to the full houses of parliament.
"At best what we have is an empty box, deprived of any constitutional credibility, where everyone will now seek to put their own preferences," La Stampa daily said in an editorial.
